ch01.summary: The overture to the whole book: the true Dao cannot be fully grasped by words or concepts. From non-being one can watch the Dao's subtlety, from being one can watch its outline; the two come from one source, deep and mysterious, the gateway to all that is subtle.
ch01.translation:
A Dao that can be spoken is not the constant Dao; a name that can be named is not the constant name. The nameless is the beginning of heaven and earth; the named is the mother of the ten thousand things.
So always free of desire, one may watch its subtlety; always with desire, one may watch its boundary. These two come from the same source and differ only in name; together they are called the Mystery. Mystery upon mystery - the gate of all that is subtle.

glossary.en: dao - the Dao (the Way)
glossary.note: The central idea of Laozi's thought: the source of all things and the pattern by which they move. It has no form and no name, yet it is the ground of all coming-to-be and change.

glossary.en: chang - constant
glossary.note: Lasting, unchanging. The Mawangdui silk manuscript has a different character, 'heng', which Han scribes changed to 'chang' to avoid the personal name of Emperor Wen of Han.

glossary.en: miao yu jiao - the subtle and the boundary
glossary.note: 'Miao' is the subtle essence and 'jiao' is the edge or outline (some read it as 'destination'); they correspond to the two ways of watching, through non-being and through being.

glossary.en: xuan - the Mystery
glossary.note: Deep, far-reaching and hard to put into words: a word used to describe the Dao.

glossary.en: duanju yidu - another way of punctuating
glossary.note: Some read it as 'always without, in order to watch its subtlety; always with, in order to watch its boundary' (Wang Anshi, Sima Guang and others). Here the reading of Heshang Gong and Wang Bi is followed.

ch01.background: This is the first chapter of the Daodejing. In Wang Bi's edition the book opens with the Dao part (37 chapters), followed by the De part (44 chapters).

ch02.summary: Opposite ideas give rise to and complete each other. So the sage handles affairs by non-action and teaches without words, helping the ten thousand things to grow without claiming credit.
ch02.translation:
When all the world knows beauty as beauty, ugliness has already come into being. When all know the good as good, what is not good has already come into being.
So being and non-being give birth to each other, hard and easy complete each other, long and short measure each other, high and low lean on each other, tone and voice harmonise with each other, before and after follow each other.
Therefore the sage deals with affairs through non-action and carries out the teaching that uses no words. The ten thousand things arise, and he does not turn them away. He gives them life without owning them, acts without relying on it, and when the work is done does not dwell in it. Because he does not dwell in it, it never leaves him.

glossary.en: xiangdui xiangsheng - opposites give rise to each other
glossary.note: Every idea exists only because of its opposite, so distinctions are relative and not absolute.

glossary.en: wuwei - non-action (wuwei)
glossary.note: Not acting rashly or against the grain of nature. It does not mean doing nothing; it means following the nature of things and not forcing anything.

glossary.en: bu yan zhi jiao - teaching without words
glossary.note: Teaching that does not rely on speech and commands, but works quietly by example.

glossary.en: fu ju - not dwelling in it
glossary.note: Not claiming credit. 'When the work is done, do not dwell in it' became a famous Daoist saying about how to live.

ch03.summary: The way to govern is not to exalt the worthy, not to prize goods, and not to display what can be desired, so the people's hearts stay at peace. The sage governs by non-action, and the world is well ordered of itself.
ch03.translation:
Do not exalt the worthy, and the people will not contend. Do not prize goods that are hard to get, and the people will not become thieves. Do not show what can be desired, and the people's hearts will not be disturbed.
Therefore the sage governs by emptying their hearts and filling their bellies, weakening their ambitions and strengthening their bones. He keeps the people always without cunning and without desire, and makes the clever not dare to act. Practise non-action, and nothing is left ungoverned.

glossary.en: shang xian - exalting the worthy
glossary.note: Honouring the worthy and competing over a reputation for worth. What Laozi opposes is the contention this brings, not worthy people themselves.

glossary.en: xu qi xin, shi qi fu - empty the heart, fill the belly
glossary.note: To empty the heart is to drop cleverness and idle thoughts; to fill the belly is to make sure the people are fed. It leans towards a simple, life-nourishing way of government.

glossary.en: wei wuwei - practise non-action
glossary.note: To act in the manner of non-action: follow nature and do not force.

glossary.en: wu zhi wu yu - without cunning and without desire
glossary.note: This does not mean keeping people stupid, but making them less clever and less greedy so that they stay simple.

ch04.summary: The body of the Dao is empty, yet its working is inexhaustible; it seems the ancestor of the ten thousand things. It blunts what is sharp, unties what is tangled, softens the glare and joins the dust; deep and clear, it seems to be there, and it came before the Lord.
ch04.translation:
The Dao is empty, yet in use it seems never to be filled. Fathomless, it seems the ancestor of the ten thousand things.
It blunts the sharp, unties the tangled, softens the glare, joins the dust. Deep and clear, it seems somehow to exist.
I do not know whose child it is; it seems to come before the Lord.

glossary.en: chong - empty
glossary.note: Empty, hollow. One reading takes it as the same as 'zhong', an empty vessel; the silk manuscript has 'zhong'.

glossary.term: 挫其銳，解其紛，和其光，同其塵
glossary.en: cuo qi rui, jie qi fen, he qi guang, tong qi chen - blunt the sharp, untie the tangled, soften the glare, join the dust
glossary.note: A picture of the Dao's humility and harmony, and also a Daoist way of living: do not show your edge, and mix with the world.

glossary.en: xiang di zhi xian - before the Lord
glossary.note: 'Xiang' means 'seems', and 'di' is the Lord, the supreme god of Heaven. It says that the Dao existed before any personal god.

glossary.en: zhan - deep and clear
glossary.note: Clear and deep, and so quiet and far-reaching.

ch04.background: The line 'blunt the sharp, untie the tangled, soften the glare, join the dust' appears again in chapter 56, and commentators have long suspected that one of the two is a displaced passage.

ch05.summary: Heaven and earth have no favourites, and the sage has no private feeling. Between heaven and earth is like a bellows, empty and never exhausted. Many words quickly lead to poverty, so it is better to hold to the empty centre.
ch05.translation:
Heaven and earth are not humane; they treat the ten thousand things as straw dogs. The sage is not humane; he treats the people as straw dogs.
The space between heaven and earth - is it not like a bellows? Empty, yet it does not collapse; the more it moves, the more comes out.
Many words soon come to their limit; it is better to hold to the centre.

glossary.en: bu ren - not humane
glossary.note: Not favouring anyone and not granting special kindness. It means treating all alike and following nature; it does not mean being cruel.

glossary.en: chugou - straw dogs
glossary.note: Dogs made of straw and used in sacrifice, thrown away afterwards. They stand for the way heaven and earth show no special favour to the ten thousand things.

glossary.en: tuoyue - bellows
glossary.note: A bellows of ancient times: 'tuo' is the skin bag, 'yue' the tube the air goes through. It pictures heaven and earth, empty and yet able to bring things forth.

glossary.en: shou zhong - hold to the centre
glossary.note: One reading takes 'zhong' as 'chong', emptiness, so it means keeping to the empty; another takes it as the state of being upright. Either way it means holding to inner emptiness and stillness.

ch06.summary: The 'valley spirit' and the 'mysterious female' picture the power of the Dao to bring things into being: it is unbroken and never used up.
ch06.translation: The valley spirit does not die; this is called the mysterious female. The gate of the mysterious female is called the root of heaven and earth. Unbroken, it seems to exist; use it, and it never wears out.

glossary.en: gushen - the valley spirit
glossary.note: A valley is empty and 'shen' is spiritual and marvellous: a picture of the Dao's empty and inexhaustible power to give life. Heshang Gong, however, reads it as the spirits of the five organs.

glossary.en: xuanpin - the mysterious female
glossary.note: 'Xuan' is deep and mysterious, 'pin' is the female organ of birth: a picture of the Dao's power of bringing things forth.

glossary.en: tiandi gen - the root of heaven and earth
glossary.note: The source from which heaven and earth come.

glossary.en: bu qin - never wears out
glossary.note: Does not tire and is not exhausted; one reading takes 'qin' as meaning 'exhausted'.

ch07.summary: Heaven and earth last because they do not live for themselves. The sage likewise gains by not putting himself first or acting for himself.
ch07.translation:
Heaven is long and earth is lasting. The reason heaven and earth can be long and lasting is that they do not live for themselves, and so they can live long.
Therefore the sage puts himself last and comes first; he sets himself outside, and himself is preserved. Is it not because he has no private interest that he can fulfil his own interest?

glossary.en: bu zi sheng - not living for oneself
glossary.note: Not working for one's own survival, having no selfish heart.

glossary.en: hou qi shen er shen xian - putting oneself last and coming first
glossary.note: By placing oneself behind others one is put in front by them: an example of 'the soft overcomes the hard'.

glossary.en: wai qi shen - setting oneself outside
glossary.note: Taking oneself lightly and leaving oneself out of account.

glossary.en: cheng qi si - fulfilling one's own interest
glossary.note: The result is that having no self-interest brings one's own interest; it is not something sought on purpose.

ch08.summary: The highest good is like water: it benefits all things without contending, and settles in the low places people dislike, and so it is close to the Dao.
ch08.translation:
The highest good is like water. Water is good at benefiting the ten thousand things without contending. It dwells in places that people dislike, and so it is close to the Dao.
In dwelling, be good at the ground; in the heart, be good at depth; in giving, be good at humaneness; in speech, be good at trust; in government, be good at order; in affairs, be good at ability; in action, be good at timing.
Only because it does not contend, it is without blame.

glossary.en: shang shan ruo shui - the highest good is like water
glossary.note: Water is the picture Laozi uses most: softness, humility and nourishment.

glossary.en: ji yu dao - close to the Dao
glossary.note: Near to the Dao. 'Ji' means near.

glossary.en: qi shan - the seven goods
glossary.note: Dwelling, heart, giving, speech, government, affairs and action: seven sides of the virtue of water.

glossary.en: you - blame
glossary.note: Fault, and the resentment that follows it.

ch09.summary: Things should be stopped at fullness: wealth and rank with pride bring disaster, and withdrawing when the work is done is in accord with the Way of Heaven.
ch09.translation:
To hold something and keep it full is not as good as stopping. To pound it and sharpen it, you cannot keep it for long. When gold and jade fill the hall, no one can guard them. To be rich and honoured and proud is to leave a disaster for oneself.
When the work is done, withdraw oneself: this is the Way of Heaven.

glossary.en: chi er ying zhi - holding it and keeping it full
glossary.note: Holding something so that it is brim-full, a picture of the pursuit of fullness.

glossary.en: chuai er rui zhi - pounding and sharpening it
glossary.note: To hammer and grind to a point. The character 'rui' (sharp) is written differently in some texts; the silk manuscript has another character again.

glossary.en: gong sui shen tui - withdraw when the work is done
glossary.note: To retire once achievements are complete, not clinging to position. In history Fan Li and Zhang Liang are held to have done this.

glossary.en: tian zhi dao - the Way of Heaven
glossary.note: The law of nature: what is full must wane, and what is at its height must decline.

ch10.summary: Through discipline - concentrating qi to become soft, cleansing away stray thoughts, acting without forcing - one reaches mysterious virtue: giving life without owning, acting without relying, leading without ruling.
ch10.translation:
Carrying the soul and the vital spirit and embracing the One, can you keep from being parted? Gathering your qi to the point of softness, can you be like an infant? Cleansing and clearing the dark mirror, can you leave it without a flaw? Loving the people and governing the state, can you do it without cleverness? When the gates of heaven open and close, can you be like the female? Understanding all within the four directions, can you do it without acting?
Give them life, nourish them. Give life without owning, act without relying, lead without ruling: this is called mysterious virtue.

glossary.en: zai yingpo bao yi - carrying the soul and embracing the One
glossary.note: 'Zai' is a particle. 'Yingpo' means the soul and spirit (some say body and spirit). 'Embracing the One' is to become one, and some read it as holding to the Dao.

glossary.en: xuanlan - the dark mirror
glossary.note: 'Lan' is the same as 'jian', a mirror: the heart as a deep and bright mirror. The silk manuscript has a different character, 'xuanjian'.

glossary.en: tianmen kaihe - the gates of heaven opening and closing
glossary.note: One reading takes it as the opening and closing of the senses (ears, eyes, mouth and nose); another as the workings of nature; another as the mouth.

glossary.en: xuande - mysterious virtue
glossary.note: Deep and subtle virtue: giving life without owning, acting without relying, leading without ruling. The same line appears in chapter 51.

ch11.summary: What is 'there' is useful only because of what is 'not there'. The cart, the vessel and the room show the use of emptiness.
ch11.translation:
Thirty spokes share one hub; it is the empty space in the middle that makes the use of the cart. Clay is shaped into a vessel; it is the emptiness inside that makes the use of the vessel. Doors and windows are cut to make a room; it is the emptiness that makes the use of the room.
Therefore what is there gives benefit, and what is not there gives use.

glossary.en: fu, gu - spokes, hub
glossary.note: The spokes are the rods of a wheel; the hub is the wooden centre of the wheel, with a hole through which the axle passes.

glossary.en: shanzhi - to shape clay
glossary.note: To work clay with water and knead it into a vessel. 'Shan' is to knead and 'zhi' is sticky clay.

glossary.en: huyou - doors and windows
glossary.note: The door and the window.

glossary.term: 有之以為利，無之以為用
glossary.en: you zhi yi wei li, wu zhi yi wei yong - what is there gives benefit, what is not there gives use
glossary.note: Being gives form and convenience; non-being gives function. The two depend on and complete each other.

ch12.summary: Chasing sensory pleasure too far makes people lose their nature. The sage asks only for enough to eat and a quiet life, and is not greedy for pleasures of eye and ear.
ch12.translation:
The five colours make the eye blind. The five notes make the ear deaf. The five flavours spoil the palate. Racing and hunting drive the heart wild. Goods that are hard to get hinder a person's conduct.
Therefore the sage cares for the belly and not for the eye. He leaves that and takes this.

glossary.en: wuse, wuyin, wuwei - the five colours, notes and flavours
glossary.note: Blue-green, yellow, red, white, black; the five notes gong, shang, jue, zhi, yu; and sour, bitter, sweet, pungent, salty. They stand for all kinds of sensory stimulation.

glossary.en: kou shuang - spoiled palate
glossary.note: The sense of taste is damaged and cannot tell flavours. 'Shuang' means to go wrong.

glossary.en: wei fu bu wei mu - for the belly and not for the eye
glossary.note: The belly stands for basic, inner needs; the eye stands for outward temptations of the senses.

glossary.en: qu bi qu ci - leave that and take this
glossary.note: To give up the chase after outward things and keep inner contentment.

ch13.summary: Favour and disgrace both disturb us because we value our own selves too much. Only one who does not hold the self precious, and loves it as he would love the world, can be trusted with the world.
ch13.translation:
Favour and disgrace both bring alarm; honour great calamity as you honour your own body.
What does it mean that favour and disgrace both bring alarm? Favour is a low thing: gaining it brings alarm and losing it brings alarm. This is what is meant by favour and disgrace both bringing alarm.
What does it mean to honour great calamity as you honour your own body? The reason I have great calamity is that I have a body. If I had no body, what calamity could I have?
Therefore one who values his body as he would the world can be trusted with the world; one who loves his body as he would the world can be given the world to keep.

glossary.en: chong ru ruo jing - favour and disgrace both bring alarm
glossary.note: Whether in favour or in disgrace the mind is unsettled, which shows how people are pulled about by praise and blame from outside.

glossary.en: gui da huan ruo shen - honour great calamity as you honour your body
glossary.note: To count great calamity as seriously as one's own body, meaning that people suffer worry because they cling to the body.

glossary.en: chong wei xia - favour is low
glossary.note: To be favoured is to stand in a lower position. Some editions read 'disgrace is low' instead.

glossary.en: ji tianxia, tuo tianxia - to be trusted with the world, to be given the world to keep
glossary.note: To be entrusted with the world. It means that only one who does not cling to life or hold things as his own is fit to take charge of the world.

ch13.background: Readers through the ages have understood the line about valuing the body as one would the world in different ways. One reading is that only one who holds himself in high regard can be trusted with the world.

ch14.summary: The Dao cannot be grasped by the senses: it is not seen, heard or touched. It seems to be and not to be, with no head and no tail, and holding to the ancient Dao one can master the present.
ch14.translation:
Look at it and you do not see it: it is called the Plain. Listen to it and you do not hear it: it is called the Faint. Grasp it and you do not get hold of it: it is called the Subtle. These three cannot be probed to the end, and so they blend into one.
Its upper side is not bright; its lower side is not dark. Unbroken, it cannot be named, and it returns again to the state of no-thing. This is called the shape without shape, the image of no thing. This is called the dim and the vague. Go to meet it and you do not see its head; follow it and you do not see its back.
Hold to the Dao of old to manage what exists today. To be able to know the ancient beginning is called the thread of the Dao.

glossary.en: yi, xi, wei - the Plain, the Faint, the Subtle
glossary.note: Words for the Dao that cannot be seen, heard or touched. The three blend into one and describe the Dao as a whole.

glossary.en: huhuang - dim and vague
glossary.note: Indistinct, as if there and not there. It means the same as 'huanghu' in chapter 21.

glossary.en: shengsheng - unbroken
glossary.note: Stretching on without a break.

glossary.en: dao ji - the thread of the Dao
glossary.note: The guiding rule and pattern of the Dao. To grasp it is to know the origin of things.

ch15.summary: Those of old who were good at the Way were subtle, mysterious, penetrating and too deep to fathom. Their bearing was careful, simple and open; by not seeking fullness they could keep renewing themselves.
ch15.translation:
Those of old who were good at being masters were subtle, mysterious and penetrating, and so deep that they could not be understood. Because they cannot be understood, I will describe them by force:
Hesitant, like one crossing a river in winter. Wary, like one fearing his neighbours on every side. Dignified, like a guest. Loosening, like ice about to melt. Solid, like uncarved wood. Open, like a valley. Murky, like muddy water.
Who can make muddy water clear by keeping still, slowly? Who can keep still for long and slowly bring life to birth? One who holds to this Dao does not wish to be full. Only because he is not full can he wear out and yet be made anew.

glossary.en: shi - master (or 'Dao')
glossary.note: In the silk manuscript this word is 'dao', so it means someone good at following the Way.

glossary.en: weimiao xuantong - subtle, mysterious and penetrating
glossary.note: Fine and deep, reaching into what is hidden.

glossary.en: yu, you - hesitant, wary
glossary.note: The 'yu' is a beast that hesitates and takes care, and the 'you' is also a cautious, suspicious animal. Both describe someone who acts carefully.

glossary.en: bi bu xin cheng - wear out and be made anew
glossary.note: 'Bi' means worn and old. One reading takes the line as 'can be worn out and yet be made new', meaning that one renews oneself even in old age.

ch16.summary: Reach emptiness and hold to stillness, and watch the ten thousand things return to their roots. Returning to the root is returning to one's destiny; only one who knows the constant is clear, and in the end one joins the Dao and is free from danger all one's life.
ch16.translation:
Reach the utmost emptiness; keep to the deepest stillness. The ten thousand things rise together, and I watch them return. Things flourish in great numbers, and each goes back to its root.
Going back to the root is called stillness. This is called returning to one's destiny. Returning to destiny is called the constant. Knowing the constant is called clarity. Not knowing the constant, one acts blindly and meets disaster.
Knowing the constant, one is all-embracing; all-embracing, one is impartial; impartial, one is complete; complete, one is in accord with Heaven; in accord with Heaven, one is in accord with the Dao; in accord with the Dao, one lasts. To the end of one's life, one is free from danger.

glossary.en: zhi xu ji, shou jing du - reach utmost emptiness, hold to deep stillness
glossary.note: To take emptiness and stillness as far as they go and keep to them firmly: Laozi's practice of cultivation.

glossary.en: fu - to return
glossary.note: To go round and come back. Things that have grown must in the end go back to their source, showing that 'returning is the movement of the Dao'.

glossary.en: fu ming - returning to destiny
glossary.note: Going back to the nature of one's life (ming).

glossary.en: chang, ming - the constant, clarity
glossary.note: The constant is the unchanging law; clarity is the wisdom that sees through to it.

ch17.summary: The best ruler is one whom the people barely know exists; next comes one they love and praise, then one they fear, and the worst is one they despise. The ideal government is one where, when the work is done, the people say 'it happened naturally'.
ch17.translation:
The best rulers: the people below only know that they exist. The next: the people love them and praise them. The next: the people fear them. The next: the people despise them.
Where trust is not enough, there will be distrust. How carefully he speaks, and values his words! When the work is done and affairs are completed, the people all say: "We did it by ourselves, naturally."

glossary.en: taishang - the best
glossary.note: The highest class, the highest state.

glossary.en: xia zhi you zhi - the people below know that they exist
glossary.note: The people only know there is a ruler and do not feel his influence. Some editions read 'do not know that they exist', so that the people do not know of any ruler at all.

glossary.en: gui yan - value words
glossary.note: Be careful of speech and give few commands.

glossary.en: ziran - naturally, of itself
glossary.note: Being so of itself, not forced from outside.

ch18.summary: Only after the great Dao is abandoned is there need for humaneness and rightness; only when cleverness appears does deceit appear; only when families are at odds is there talk of filial piety; only when the state is in chaos are there loyal ministers.
ch18.translation: When the great Dao is abandoned, there is humaneness and rightness. When cleverness appears, there is great deceit. When the six family relations are not in harmony, there are filial piety and parental kindness. When the state is in darkness and chaos, there are loyal ministers.

glossary.en: da dao fei, you ren yi - when the great Dao is abandoned, there is humaneness and rightness
glossary.note: It is only because morality has fallen that humaneness and rightness stand out as needed. Laozi uses this to criticise virtue that is displayed on purpose.

glossary.en: da wei - great deceit
glossary.note: Serious falseness and trickery.

glossary.en: liuqin - the six relations
glossary.note: Father and son, elder and younger brother, husband and wife; or more generally all relatives.

glossary.en: yu sanshiba zhang huying - an echo of chapter 38
glossary.note: The chapter is a reflection: the displaying of virtue presupposes a loss of virtue, in the same spirit as 'after the Dao is lost, there is virtue' in chapter 38.

ch18.background: This chapter and chapter 19 criticise the Confucian virtues of humaneness, rightness, ritual propriety and wisdom. The Guodian bamboo-slip version reads 'when the old great Dao was abandoned, how could there be humaneness and rightness', which is milder in tone.

ch19.summary: It argues for cutting off sageliness and cleverness, discarding humaneness and rightness, and cutting off skill and profit, and returning to simplicity: show plainness, embrace the uncarved, have little self-interest and few desires.
ch19.translation:
Cut off sageliness and discard cleverness, and the people will benefit a hundredfold. Cut off humaneness and discard rightness, and the people will return to filial piety and kindness. Cut off skill and discard profit, and robbers and thieves will be no more.
These three sayings, taken as mere adornment, are not enough. So let there be something people can hold to: show plainness, embrace the uncarved block, have little self-interest and few desires.

glossary.en: jue sheng qi zhi - cut off sageliness, discard cleverness
glossary.note: To get rid of the sageliness and wisdom that are held up on purpose. It does not deny true wisdom. The Guodian slip version reads 'cut off cleverness, discard argument'.

glossary.en: jue ren qi yi - cut off humaneness, discard rightness
glossary.note: As above. The Warring States slip version reads 'cut off falseness, discard scheming', which is milder.

glossary.en: jian su bao pu - show plainness, embrace the uncarved
glossary.note: Outwardly plain, inwardly holding to simplicity: the ideal Daoist character.

glossary.en: shao si gua yu - few private aims, few desires
glossary.note: To reduce selfishness and desire.

ch19.background: The Guodian bamboo-slip version of this chapter differs a great deal from the received text. Many scholars think the received text is a later revision from the late Warring States period, in a much harsher tone.

ch20.summary: Setting the crowd against himself, Laozi draws one who has the Dao as someone who seems dull and alone. He does not follow the fashion, and values 'feeding from the Mother', which is holding to the Dao.
ch20.translation:
Cut off learning and there is no worry. 'Yes' and 'yeah' - how far apart are they? Good and evil - how far apart are they? What people fear, one cannot help but fear.
How wasteful and endless it is! The crowd are merry, as if feasting on the great sacrifice, as if climbing a terrace in spring. I alone am quiet, giving no sign, like an infant who has not yet smiled; so weary, as if I had nowhere to return to. The crowd all have more than enough, and I alone seem to have lost everything. I have the heart of a fool indeed - how muddled!
Ordinary people are bright; I alone am dim. Ordinary people are sharp; I alone am dull. Calm like the sea, blowing as if it will never stop. The crowd all have some purpose, and I alone am stubborn, like a rustic.
I alone am different from others, and I value feeding from the Mother.

glossary.en: jue xue wu you - cut off learning and there is no worry
glossary.note: Without the learning of the world (the learning of cleverness) there is no trouble. Some put this line at the end of the previous chapter.

glossary.en: wei yu e - 'yes' and 'yeah'
glossary.note: 'Wei' is a respectful reply and 'e' is a rude one. It is a picture of how worldly distinctions are relative.

glossary.en: tailao - the great sacrifice
glossary.note: The most solemn of ancient sacrifices, with ox, sheep and pig. 'Feasting on the great sacrifice' stands for the crowd's merriment.

glossary.en: shi mu - feeding from the Mother
glossary.note: 'Shi' is to draw nourishment and 'mother' is the Dao. To value it is to prize the nourishment one gets from the Dao.

ch21.summary: A person of great virtue follows only the Dao. The Dao is dim and hard to see, yet within it are image, thing, essence and trust, the ground of the beginnings of all things.
ch21.translation:
The form of great virtue follows the Dao alone. The Dao as a thing is only vague and dim. Dim and vague, yet within it is an image; vague and dim, yet within it is a thing. Deep and dark, yet within it is an essence; this essence is very real, and within it is trust.
From now back to antiquity, its name has never gone away, and through it we survey the beginnings of all things. How do I know what the beginnings of all things are like? By this.

glossary.en: kongde - great virtue
glossary.note: 'Kong' means great or very, so 'kongde' is great virtue.

glossary.en: huanghu - dim and vague
glossary.note: Seeming to be and not to be, and hard to pin down: a picture of how the Dao cannot be put into words.

glossary.en: yaoming - deep and dark
glossary.note: Far-reaching and dim, a picture of the Dao's depth.

glossary.en: zhongfu - the beginnings of all things
glossary.note: 'Fu' is the same as 'father', and one reading takes it as 'beginning'. The word means the origin of the ten thousand things.

ch22.summary: Through the bent, the crooked, the hollow and the worn, the chapter shows that what is soft and low in the end achieves completion. The sage does not show off or assert himself, and so he becomes clear, has merit and lasts.
ch22.translation:
The bent is made whole. The crooked is made straight. The hollow is filled. The worn is made new. Having little, one gains; having much, one is confused.
Therefore the sage embraces the One as a model for the world. Not showing himself, he is clear. Not asserting himself, he is distinguished. Not boasting, he has merit. Not being proud, he lasts. Only because he does not contend, no one in the world can contend with him.
What the ancients called 'the bent is made whole' - were these empty words? Truly, wholeness returns to him.

glossary.en: qu ze quan - the bent is made whole
glossary.note: By bending and yielding, one is kept whole. Laozi uses reversed sayings to show the strength of the soft.

glossary.en: bao yi - embrace the One
glossary.note: To hold to the Dao. 'The One' is the Dao.

glossary.en: zi xian - showing oneself
glossary.note: Putting oneself forward and parading. The character stands for the word meaning to appear.

glossary.en: bu zi fa - not boasting
glossary.note: Not praising one's own achievements. 'Fa' is to brag.

ch23.summary: Speaking little accords with nature; even whirlwind and downpour do not last. Those who follow the Dao are at one with the Dao, with virtue or with loss, and where trust is lacking, people do not trust.
ch23.translation:
To speak little is natural. So a whirlwind does not last a morning, and a sudden downpour does not last a day. Who makes these? Heaven and earth. If heaven and earth cannot make them last, how much less can a human being?
So one who follows the Dao in his work: one who is of the Dao is at one with the Dao; one who is of virtue is at one with virtue; one who is of loss is at one with loss. When one is at one with the Dao, the Dao is glad to receive him. When one is at one with virtue, virtue is glad to receive him. When one is at one with loss, loss is glad to receive him.
Where trust is not enough, there is distrust.

glossary.en: xi yan - speak little
glossary.note: To speak little, meaning to give few commands. 'Xi' means rare.

glossary.en: piaofeng, zhouyu - whirlwind, downpour
glossary.note: Violent wind and rain cannot last, and so they picture a harsh government that cannot endure.

glossary.en: congshi yu dao zhe - one who follows the Dao in his work
glossary.note: Someone who devotes himself to the Dao.

glossary.en: xin bu zu yan, you bu xin yan - where trust is not enough, there is distrust
glossary.note: The same sentence as in chapter 17. One view holds that it is an intrusion here.

ch24.summary: Standing on tiptoe or striding does not last. Showing oneself, being self-righteous, boasting and being proud are all 'leftover food and superfluous growths' that are against the Dao.
ch24.translation:
One who stands on tiptoe does not stand firm. One who straddles does not walk well. One who shows himself is not clear. One who asserts himself is not distinguished. One who boasts has no merit. One who is proud does not last.
In the Dao, these are called leftover food and superfluous growths. Things may well despise them, so one who has the Dao does not dwell in them.

glossary.en: qi zhe bu li - one on tiptoe does not stand
glossary.note: To raise oneself on tiptoe: forced effort that cannot last.

glossary.en: kua zhe bu xing - one who straddles does not walk
glossary.note: To take wide strides; haste makes no speed.

glossary.en: yu shi zhui xing - leftover food and superfluous growths
glossary.note: Leftover food and growths on the body: pictures of excess behaviour that people dislike.

glossary.en: zi jin - being proud
glossary.note: Pride and arrogance.

ch25.summary: It describes the body of the Dao: born before heaven and earth, silent, standing alone and moving everywhere without tiring, the mother of the world. It is called Dao, or by force 'great'; humans follow earth, earth follows heaven, heaven follows the Dao, and the Dao follows what is natural.
ch25.translation:
There is something formless yet complete, born before heaven and earth. Silent and empty, it stands alone and does not change; it moves everywhere and does not tire. It can be the mother of the world.
I do not know its name. I style it 'Dao', and, forcing a name on it, I call it 'great'. Great means going; going means far; far means returning.
So the Dao is great, heaven is great, earth is great, and the king too is great. Within the realm there are four great ones, and the king is one of them.
Humans follow earth. Earth follows heaven. Heaven follows the Dao. The Dao follows what is natural.

glossary.en: you wu huncheng - something formless yet complete
glossary.note: There is something that is whole by its own nature, meaning the Dao.

glossary.en: zi zhi yue dao - style it 'Dao'
glossary.note: 'Zi' is a style name, 'ming' is a name: to call it 'Dao' only for want of a better word.

glossary.en: sida - the four great
glossary.note: Dao, heaven, earth and the king (or 'person'). Wang Bi's text reads 'the king is also great'; the silk manuscript and the Fu Yi edition read 'king', and Heshang Gong's edition reads 'person'.

glossary.en: Dao fa ziran - the Dao follows what is natural
glossary.note: The Dao takes naturalness as its model. This does not mean there is a 'nature' above the Dao; it means that the Dao's own nature is to be natural and without forcing.

ch26.summary: The heavy is the root of the light, and stillness is the master of restlessness. A ruler must not act lightly and lose his root.
ch26.translation:
The heavy is the root of the light; stillness is the lord of restlessness. Therefore the sage, travelling all day, never leaves his baggage wagons. Though there are splendid sights, he stays calm and aloof.
How can the ruler of ten thousand chariots treat his own person lightly in the eyes of the world? If light, he loses his root; if restless, he loses his throne.

glossary.en: zizhong - baggage wagons
glossary.note: The carts that carry supplies on a march. Here they stand for the weighty foundation one must not leave.

glossary.en: yanchu - to stay at ease
glossary.note: To live quietly at home.

glossary.en: rongguan - splendid sights
glossary.note: Grand and glittering things, meaning luxurious enjoyment.

glossary.en: wansheng zhi zhu - ruler of ten thousand chariots
glossary.note: The ruler of a great state that could field ten thousand war chariots.

ch27.summary: One who is good at acting leaves no trace. The sage is good at saving people and things, so that no one and nothing is wasted. The good person is the teacher of the not-good, and the not-good is the material of the good.
ch27.translation:
Good walking leaves no tracks. Good speech has no flaw to find fault with. Good counting uses no counting rods. Good closing uses no bolt or bar, yet cannot be opened. Good tying uses no cord, yet cannot be undone.
Therefore the sage is always good at saving people, and so no one is cast aside; always good at saving things, and so nothing is cast aside. This is called following the light.
So the good person is the teacher of the not-good person, and the not-good person is the material for the good person. One who does not value his teacher or love his material, though clever, is greatly lost. This is called the essential mystery.

glossary.en: zheji - wheel tracks
glossary.note: The marks of cart wheels.

glossary.en: chouce - counting rods
glossary.note: Small bamboo rods used for calculating in ancient times.

glossary.en: xi ming - following the light
glossary.note: 'Xi' is to carry on or to hold within, and 'ming' is clear wisdom: to keep one's light within and not show it.

glossary.en: zi - material
glossary.note: Something to draw on or learn from. It means that even the not-good person gives the good person something to be warned by.

ch28.summary: Know the male but hold to the female, know the white but hold to the black, know glory but hold to disgrace: by being the ravine, the pattern and the valley of the world through softness and humility, one returns to the infant, the limitless and the uncarved. When the uncarved is cut up it becomes vessels, and the sage uses them as chief of officials.
ch28.translation:
Know the male, hold to the female: be the ravine of the world. Being the ravine of the world, constant virtue does not leave, and one returns to being an infant.
Know the white, hold to the black: be the pattern of the world. Being the pattern of the world, constant virtue does not err, and one returns to the limitless.
Know glory, hold to disgrace: be the valley of the world. Being the valley of the world, constant virtue is sufficient, and one returns to the uncarved.
When the uncarved is cut up, it becomes vessels. The sage uses them and becomes chief of officials. Therefore the great carving does not cut.

glossary.en: xiong yu ci - male and female
glossary.note: The male stands for strength and advance, the female for gentleness and humility. Laozi advises knowing the male but keeping to the female.

glossary.en: xi, gu - ravine, valley
glossary.note: A stream and a valley lie low and take in many waters, a picture of humility that contains.

glossary.en: pu - the uncarved
glossary.note: A block of wood not yet carved, a picture of the natural, original state of the Dao.

glossary.en: da zhi bu ge - the great carving does not cut
glossary.note: The most complete order is not cut up, and keeps its wholeness and naturalness.

ch29.summary: The world is a sacred thing and cannot be forced. Whoever forces or grasps it fails; the sage puts away the extreme, the extravagant and the excessive.
ch29.translation:
If you want to take the world and act upon it, I see that you will not succeed. The world is a sacred vessel and cannot be acted upon. Whoever acts upon it ruins it; whoever grasps it loses it.
Among things, some go ahead and some follow; some breathe softly and some blow hard; some are strong and some weak; some are broken and some toppled. Therefore the sage rejects the extreme, the extravagant and the excessive.

glossary.en: shenqi - sacred vessel
glossary.note: A sacred object, meaning the power to rule the world; a picture of the world as something that cannot be taken by force.

glossary.en: wei zhe bai zhi, zhi zhe shi zhi - whoever acts on it ruins it, whoever grasps it loses it
glossary.note: Forced action is bound to fail, and clinging is bound to lose.

glossary.en: xu, chui - breathe softly, blow hard
glossary.note: One breathes out slowly and the other blows quickly: a picture of how things differ in their natures.

glossary.en: qu shen, qu she, qu tai - reject the extreme, the extravagant, the excessive
glossary.note: To get rid of what goes too far, what is lavish and what is arrogant, and so keep to moderation.

ch30.summary: One who helps a ruler with the Dao does not dominate the world by force of arms. War brings evil results, and even in victory one should not boast, for what has reached its peak turns back.
ch30.translation:
One who assists a ruler with the Dao does not use weapons to dominate the world. Such things tend to come back. Where an army has camped, thorns and brambles grow. After a great war, there are always years of famine.
A good commander gets his result and stops; he does not dare to use it to take strength. Get the result, but do not be proud of it. Get the result, but do not boast. Get the result, but do not be arrogant. Get the result because you had no choice. Get the result, but do not use force.
When things are strong they grow old. This is called being against the Dao, and what is against the Dao comes early to its end.

glossary.en: hao huan - tends to come back
glossary.note: Likely to bring retribution; 'huan' means to return.

glossary.en: guo - to achieve the result
glossary.note: To reach the desired effect, to succeed. Laozi says one should stop once the aim is reached and not use force to show strength.

glossary.en: jin, fa, jiao - pride, boasting, arrogance
glossary.note: Self-importance, bragging and arrogance: the states of mind that arise easily after a victory.

glossary.en: wu zhuang ze lao - when things are strong they grow old
glossary.note: After a thing is in its prime it turns towards old age.

ch31.summary: Weapons are instruments of ill omen, and a noble person uses them only when he has no choice and does not praise victory. When many have been killed they should be met with the rites of mourning.
ch31.translation:
Fine weapons are instruments of ill omen. Things may well hate them, so one who has the Dao does not dwell among them.
The noble person at home honours the left; in war he honours the right. Weapons are instruments of ill omen, not the instruments of the noble person. When he has no choice but to use them, calm and plain restraint is best. Victory is nothing to praise; to praise it is to delight in killing people. One who delights in killing people cannot succeed in the world.
In happy affairs the left is honoured; in sad affairs the right. The lieutenant general stands on the left; the commanding general stands on the right - which is to say, they are placed as at a funeral. When many people have been killed, one should weep for them with grief. A victory in war should be treated with the rites of mourning.

glossary.en: jia bing - fine weapons
glossary.note: Excellent weapons. Another reading takes 'jia' as a loan for a word meaning 'only', so that it means 'delighting in war'.

glossary.en: gui zuo, gui you - honour the left, honour the right
glossary.note: The ancients held the left to be yang and life and the right yin and killing; so the left was honoured in peacetime, and the right in war.

glossary.en: tiandan - calm and plain
glossary.note: Calm and not greedy.

glossary.en: yi sangli chu zhi - treat it with the rites of mourning
glossary.note: Even a victory is to be treated as a funeral, showing reverence for life.

ch31.background: Some sentences in this chapter, such as those from 'in happy affairs the left is honoured' to the end, are thought to be an old commentary that got mixed into the text.

ch32.summary: The Dao is constant and nameless, simple. If lords and kings can hold to it, the ten thousand things will come to them of themselves. Once a system is set up there are names, and one must know where to stop in order to be safe.
ch32.translation:
The Dao is constant and nameless. Though the uncarved is small, no one in the world can make it a subject. If lords and kings could hold to it, the ten thousand things would come to them of themselves.
Heaven and earth unite and send down sweet dew; the people, with no one commanding them, are even of themselves.
When the system first begins, there are names. Once there are names, one must also know where to stop. Knowing where to stop is how to avoid danger.
The Dao in the world is like the valley streams to the rivers and the sea.

glossary.en: pu - the uncarved
glossary.note: A block of wood not yet carved, a picture of the original nature of the Dao.

glossary.en: bin - to submit
glossary.note: To come as a guest, to submit and give allegiance.

glossary.en: shi zhi you ming - when the system begins there are names
glossary.note: When people first set up systems and titles.

glossary.en: zhi zhi - to know where to stop
glossary.note: To know when enough is enough: the virtue of restraint and self-reflection.

ch33.summary: Through knowing others and knowing oneself, overcoming others and overcoming oneself, contentment, perseverance, keeping one's place and not perishing in death, the chapter says what true wisdom, strength, wealth and long life are.
ch33.translation:
One who knows others is clever; one who knows himself is clear. One who overcomes others has force; one who overcomes himself is strong.
One who knows contentment is rich. One who presses on has purpose. One who does not lose his place lasts long. One who dies and yet does not perish has long life.

glossary.en: zizhi zhe ming - one who knows himself is clear
glossary.note: Knowing oneself is real understanding, and 'clarity' is a step above 'cleverness'.

glossary.en: zisheng zhe qiang - one who overcomes himself is strong
glossary.note: The one who can overcome his own selfish desires is the strongest.

glossary.en: zhizu zhe fu - one who knows contentment is rich
glossary.note: Content with what one has, one is rich within.

glossary.en: si er bu wang zhe shou - one who dies and does not perish has long life
glossary.note: One whose virtue, Dao or spirit lasts after death is truly long-lived. Another reading is 'dies and is not forgotten' (the silk manuscript has 'forgotten').

ch34.summary: The great Dao spreads everywhere; the ten thousand things live by it and it does not refuse them. It does its work without claiming it and nourishes all without being their master, and so it can be great.
ch34.translation:
The great Dao overflows; it can go to the left and to the right. The ten thousand things rely on it for life and it does not turn them away. When its work is done, it does not claim to own it.
It clothes and nourishes the ten thousand things and does not act as their master. Always without desire, it may be called small. The ten thousand things return to it and it does not act as their master; it may be called great.
Because to the end it does not make itself great, it can accomplish its greatness.

glossary.en: fan - to overflow
glossary.note: A variant of the character for spreading widely.

glossary.en: yi yang - to clothe and nourish
glossary.note: To cover and feed. 'Yi' here is a verb, meaning to drape over.

glossary.en: bu wei zhu - not acting as master
glossary.note: Not ruling over things and not possessing them.

glossary.en: keming yu xiao, keming wei da - may be called small, may be called great
glossary.note: The Dao has no desire and does not show itself, so it can be called small; the ten thousand things return to it, so it can also be called great.

ch35.summary: When a person holds the great Dao, the world comes to him without harm. Music and food stop a passing guest only for a time, but the Dao is plain and without taste, and yet it cannot be used up.
ch35.translation:
Hold the great image, and the world comes to you. They come and are not harmed; there is peace, calm and ease.
Music and good food make a passing guest stop. But the Dao when it comes out of the mouth is plain and without taste. Look at it, and it is not enough to see; listen to it, and it is not enough to hear; use it, and it cannot be used up.

glossary.en: daxiang - the great image
glossary.note: The image of the great Dao, that is, the Dao itself.

glossary.en: an ping tai - peace, calm and ease
glossary.note: Settled, peaceful and well.

glossary.en: yue yu er - music and food
glossary.note: Music and good food: a picture of sensory pleasure, set against the Dao that is 'plain and without taste'.

glossary.en: yong zhi bu zu ji - use it and it cannot be used up
glossary.note: It cannot be exhausted. 'Ji' means to use up.

ch36.summary: When things reach their limit they turn back: what is to be shrunk must first be stretched. This is subtle insight; the soft and weak overcome the hard and strong, and the sharp instruments of a state must not be shown.
ch36.translation:
What is to be shrunk must first be stretched. What is to be weakened must first be strengthened. What is to be abolished must first be raised up. What is to be taken away must first be given.
This is called subtle insight. The soft and weak overcome the hard and strong.
A fish must not leave the deep; the sharp instruments of a state must not be shown to people.

glossary.en: xi - to draw in
glossary.note: To contract, to shrink.

glossary.en: weiming - subtle insight
glossary.note: A principle that is hidden yet clear: the law by which things change into their opposite.

glossary.en: rouruo sheng gangqiang - the soft and weak overcome the hard and strong
glossary.note: One of Laozi's central claims.

glossary.en: guo zhi liqi - the sharp instruments of a state
glossary.note: One view takes these to be the arts of power and the use of rewards and punishments, another takes them to be weapons; opinions have long differed.

ch36.background: This chapter is often misread as a handbook of scheming. The more usual view is that it explains the law that things at their extreme turn back, and does not encourage plots.

ch37.summary: The Dao does nothing and yet nothing is left undone. If lords and kings hold to it, the ten thousand things transform of themselves, and where desires stir, the nameless uncarved quiets them; with no desire and with stillness the world settles of itself.
ch37.translation:
The Dao is always without action, and yet there is nothing left undone. If lords and kings could hold to it, the ten thousand things would transform of themselves.
If, in transforming, desires should stir, I would still them with the nameless uncarved. The nameless uncarved is itself free of desire. Without desire, there is stillness, and the world will settle of itself.

glossary.en: wuwei er wu bu wei - without action, yet nothing left undone
glossary.note: The Dao does nothing on purpose, and yet it accomplishes everything.

glossary.en: zi hua - transform of themselves
glossary.note: To grow and change of themselves.

glossary.en: wuming zhi pu - the nameless uncarved
glossary.note: The simple state that has no name; the original nature of the Dao.

glossary.en: zi ding - settle of themselves
glossary.note: To become calm by themselves.

ch37.background: This is the last chapter of the Dao part (the first part) in Wang Bi's edition; the second part, the De part, begins with chapter 38, 'the highest virtue is not virtuous'. The chapter is about non-action and the uncarved: if the ruler holds to the Dao, the ten thousand things transform of themselves, and even desires are quieted by the nameless uncarved.

ch38.summary: The highest virtue does not think itself virtuous and so has virtue. After the Dao is lost there is virtue, then humaneness, then rightness, then ritual; ritual is a thinning of loyalty and trust and the beginning of disorder.
ch38.translation:
The highest virtue is not virtuous, and therefore it has virtue. The lowest virtue never lets go of virtue, and therefore it has no virtue.
The highest virtue does not act and has no reason to act. The lowest virtue acts and has a reason to act. The highest humaneness acts and has no reason to act. The highest rightness acts and has a reason to act. The highest ritual acts, and when no one responds, it rolls up its sleeves and forces people.
So when the Dao is lost, there is virtue; when virtue is lost, there is humaneness; when humaneness is lost, there is rightness; when rightness is lost, there is ritual. Ritual is the thin edge of loyalty and trust, and the beginning of disorder. Foreknowledge is the flower of the Dao, and the beginning of folly.
Therefore the great person dwells in the thick and not the thin; he dwells in the fruit and not the flower. So he leaves that and takes this.

glossary.en: shang de bu de - the highest virtue is not virtuous
glossary.note: The highest virtue does not think itself virtuous. It follows nature, and therefore it has virtue.

glossary.en: shi dao er hou de - when the Dao is lost, there is virtue
glossary.note: The levels go down step by step: Dao, virtue, humaneness, rightness, ritual, each a loss of the one before.

glossary.en: qianshi - foreknowledge
glossary.note: Prior knowledge and fixed judgements; what the world calls wisdom, which Laozi sees as the showy flower of the Dao.

glossary.en: rang bi er reng zhi - roll up the sleeves and force
glossary.note: To bare the arm and pull people by force: the compulsion of ritual when it cannot move people.

ch38.background: This is the first chapter of the De part (the second part); the name Daodejing 'Classic of the Dao and De' comes from this. The Mawangdui silk manuscript puts the De part before the Dao part.

ch39.summary: Everything that has attained the One is what it is: Heaven is clear, earth calm, spirits divine, the valley full, the ten thousand things alive, and lords and kings the standard of the world. The noble takes the humble as root, and the high takes the low as foundation.
ch39.translation:
Of those in the past who attained the One: Heaven attained the One and became clear. Earth attained the One and became calm. Spirits attained the One and became divine. The valley attained the One and became full. The ten thousand things attained the One and came to life. Lords and kings attained the One and became the standard for the world.
Taken to the limit: if Heaven had nothing to make it clear, it might split. If earth had nothing to make it calm, it might erupt. If spirits had nothing to make them divine, they might fade. If the valley had nothing to make it full, it might run dry. If the ten thousand things had nothing to make them live, they might perish. If lords and kings had nothing to make them noble and high, they might fall.
So the noble takes the humble as its root, and the high takes the low as its foundation. That is why lords and kings call themselves the Orphan, the Lonely One and the Unworthy. Is this not taking the humble as the root? Is it not?
Therefore, count the parts of a carriage one by one and there is no carriage. Do not wish to gleam like jade; be rather like rough stone.

glossary.en: yi - the One
glossary.note: The Dao, or the whole, harmony and unity of the Dao. Heaven, earth and all things are what they are by attaining the One.

glossary.en: zhen - standard
glossary.note: A leader or what is upright; some editions write 'zheng', upright.

glossary.en: gu, gua, bugu - the Orphan, the Lonely One, the Unworthy
glossary.note: Humble terms kings used of themselves in ancient times, meaning lonely, of little virtue and not good.

glossary.en: zhi shu yu wu yu - count the carriage parts and there is no carriage
glossary.note: One reading is that 'shu yu' means the parts of a carriage, which if taken apart leave no carriage. It pictures how chasing after honour can leave one with nothing.

glossary.en: lulu, luoluo - gleaming, rough
glossary.note: 'Lulu' is the gleam of fine jade, 'luoluo' the hardness of stone.

ch40.summary: The movement of the Dao is a cycle of return, and its use is softness. The ten thousand things are born from being, and being is born from non-being.
ch40.translation:
Returning is the movement of the Dao. Weakness is the use of the Dao.
The ten thousand things under heaven are born from being, and being is born from non-being.

glossary.en: fan zhe dao zhi dong - returning is the movement of the Dao
glossary.note: 'Fan' means both to return and to turn into the opposite. It says that things turning into their opposites and going round and round is the movement of the Dao.

glossary.en: ruo zhe dao zhi yong - weakness is the use of the Dao
glossary.note: Softness is the way the Dao is put to use.

glossary.en: you sheng yu wu - being is born from non-being
glossary.note: The ten thousand things come from visible 'being', and visible being comes from invisible 'non-being'. Here 'non-being' is not mere nothingness but the Dao that has not yet appeared.

ch40.background: This chapter is short but is often treated as the outline of Laozi's metaphysics. The line 'being is born from non-being' later became the basis for the Wei-Jin Mysterious Learning school that honoured non-being.

ch41.summary: The highest, middling and lowest sort of people respond differently on hearing the Dao. The Dao often takes the shape of its opposite, as in 'the great sound is faint' and 'the great image has no form'; it is hidden and nameless, yet good at beginning and at completing.
ch41.translation:
When the highest sort of person hears of the Dao, he diligently practises it. When the middling sort hears of the Dao, it seems to him to be there and not there. When the lowest sort hears of the Dao, he laughs loudly at it. If he did not laugh, it would not be fit to be the Dao.
So the old sayings have it: The bright Way seems dark. The way forward seems to go back. The level way seems rough. The highest virtue seems like a valley. The greatest purity seems sullied. Broad virtue seems not enough. Established virtue seems stolen. True substance seems to change. The great square has no corners. The great vessel is completed late. The great sound is faint in sound. The great image has no form. The Dao is hidden and has no name.
Only the Dao is good at lending and at completing.

glossary.en: jianyan - old sayings
glossary.note: Sayings set down by people of old, or old proverbs.

glossary.en: yi dao ruo lei - the level way seems rough
glossary.note: The smooth Way seems to have knots in it. 'Lei' means a knot in silk.

glossary.en: da fang wu yu - the great square has no corners
glossary.note: The greatest square has no corner.

glossary.en: da qi wan cheng - the great vessel is completed late
glossary.note: The greatest vessel is finished last. The silk manuscript has a different reading, 'does not become complete'; the modern idiom takes 'completed late'.

glossary.en: da yin xi sheng - the great sound is faint in sound
glossary.note: The greatest sound is so faint it seems silent. It became a famous line in later theories of art.

ch42.summary: It gives the order in which the Dao produces the ten thousand things and the harmony of yin and yang; loss and gain complete each other, and the violent do not die a natural death.
ch42.translation:
The Dao gives birth to one. One gives birth to two. Two give birth to three. Three give birth to the ten thousand things.
The ten thousand things carry yin on their backs and embrace yang, and the blending of their qi makes harmony.
What people hate is to be called the Orphan, the Lonely One and the Unworthy, and yet kings and lords use these as their titles. So things are sometimes added to by being taken from, and sometimes taken from by being added to.
What others teach, I also teach: the violent do not die a natural death. I will take this as the father of my teaching.

glossary.en: Dao sheng yi, yi sheng er, er sheng san - the Dao gives birth to one, one to two, two to three
glossary.note: A short statement of how the cosmos came to be. Readings differ: for example one is primal qi, two is yin and yang, three is yin, yang and the harmonising qi.

glossary.en: fu yin bao yang - carry yin and embrace yang
glossary.note: All things are made of two kinds of qi, yin and yang.

glossary.en: chongqi - the blending qi
glossary.note: The harmonious qi produced when yin and yang qi stir against each other.

glossary.en: qiangliang - the violent
glossary.note: People who are overbearing and who show off their strength.

ch43.summary: The softest thing in the world can pass through the hardest; the formless can enter where there is no gap, and so we know the benefit of non-action.
ch43.translation:
The softest thing in the world gallops through the hardest thing in the world. What has no being enters where there is no gap. From this I know the benefit of non-action.
The teaching without words and the benefit of non-action - few in the world can reach them.

glossary.en: zhi rou chiping zhi jian - the softest gallops over the hardest
glossary.note: Water wearing through stone is the picture: the soft can overcome the hard.

glossary.en: wu you ru wu jian - what has no being enters where there is no gap
glossary.note: Something without form can enter a place with no gap, as air and water do.

glossary.en: bu yan zhi jiao - the teaching without words
glossary.note: See chapter 2: teaching by example.

glossary.en: xi ji - few reach
glossary.note: Few can attain it.

ch44.summary: A reminder to value life above fame and gain; by knowing contentment and knowing where to stop, one avoids disgrace and danger and lasts long.
ch44.translation:
Which is dearer, fame or the body? Which is worth more, the body or goods? Which is the greater harm, gaining or losing?
Therefore great love must bring great cost, and great hoarding must bring heavy loss. One who knows contentment is not disgraced; one who knows where to stop is not in danger, and can last long.

glossary.en: shu qin, shu duo, shu bing - which is dearer, which is more, which is the harm
glossary.note: Three pairs of contrasts that tell people to value themselves above outer things.

glossary.en: shen ai bi da fei - great love must bring great cost
glossary.note: Excessive craving leads to heavy expense.

glossary.en: zhizu bu ru, zhizhi bu dai - knowing contentment, no disgrace; knowing where to stop, no danger
glossary.note: One who knows enough is not shamed, and one who knows when to stop meets no danger.

glossary.en: duo cang bi hou wang - great hoarding brings heavy loss
glossary.note: The more one has stored up, the greater the loss when it goes.

ch45.summary: The most complete seems to lack something, the fullest seems empty, and true straightness, skill and eloquence all look like their opposites. Purity and stillness are the right way of the world.
ch45.translation:
Great completeness seems to be lacking, yet its use is never worn out. Great fullness seems empty, yet its use is never exhausted.
Great straightness seems bent, yet its use does not settle in one place. Great skill seems clumsy, yet its use never stops. Great eloquence seems halting, yet its use is never at fault. Movement overcomes cold; stillness overcomes heat. Purity and stillness are what set the world right.

glossary.en: da cheng ruo que - great completeness seems lacking
glossary.note: The greatest achievement looks as if it has gaps; because it is never self-satisfied, it can go on.

glossary.en: da qiao ruo zhuo - great skill seems clumsy
glossary.note: The finest skill looks clumsy, because it does not show off.

glossary.en: da bian ruo ne - great eloquence seems halting
glossary.note: The best debater looks as if he is poor at speaking.

glossary.en: zao sheng han, jing sheng re - movement overcomes cold, stillness overcomes heat
glossary.note: Some read it as 'stillness overcomes restlessness, cold overcomes heat' (Zhu Qianzhi and others). Here Wang Bi's text is followed.

ch46.summary: When the world has the Dao, horses work the fields; when it lacks the Dao, war horses are bred on the outskirts. The greatest calamity is not knowing contentment and the greatest fault is wanting to gain; one who knows contentment always has enough.
ch46.translation:
When the world has the Dao, swift horses are sent back to haul manure. When the world lacks the Dao, war horses are bred in the outskirts.
No calamity is greater than not knowing contentment. No fault is greater than wanting to gain. So the contentment of knowing contentment is always enough.

glossary.en: que zou ma yi fen - sending back swift horses to haul manure
glossary.note: War horses are turned back to work in the fields, hauling manure.

glossary.en: rong ma sheng yu jiao - war horses bred in the outskirts
glossary.note: Mares give birth to foals in the open country, which shows that war is constant.

glossary.en: jiu - fault
glossary.note: A mistake or calamity.

glossary.en: zhizu zhi zu, chang zu yi - the contentment of knowing contentment is always enough
glossary.note: Satisfaction that comes from being content within is lasting.

ch47.summary: One can know the world without going out of the door and know the Way of Heaven without looking out of the window. The further one goes out, the less one knows; the sage knows without travelling, understands without seeing, and accomplishes without acting.
ch47.translation:
Without going out of the door, one may know the world. Without looking out of the window, one may see the Way of Heaven. The further one goes out, the less one knows.
Therefore the sage knows without travelling, understands without seeing, and accomplishes without acting.

glossary.en: bu chu hu, zhi tianxia - without going out of the door, one knows the world
glossary.note: This does not mean that experience is not needed. It stresses that if one returns inward and embodies the Dao, all principles can be understood.

glossary.en: kui you - to look out of the window
glossary.note: To peek out through a window.

glossary.en: qi chu mi yuan, qi zhi mi shao - the further out, the less one knows
glossary.note: The more one chases outward, the easier it is to lose one's root.

glossary.en: bu jian er ming - understands without seeing
glossary.note: To understand without seeing with the eyes. 'Ming' here stands for the word meaning clear.

ch48.summary: In study, one gains day by day; in the Dao, one loses day by day. Loss upon loss reaches non-action, and with non-action nothing is left undone; to win the world, one must always be free of meddling.
ch48.translation:
In the pursuit of learning, one gains day by day. In the pursuit of the Dao, one loses day by day. Loss upon loss, until one reaches non-action. With non-action, nothing is left undone.
To win the world, always be free of meddling. Once there is meddling, one is not fit to win the world.

glossary.en: wei xue ri yi, wei dao ri sun - learning adds daily, the Dao subtracts daily
glossary.note: Learning piles up knowledge; following the Dao reduces artifice, fixed views and desires.

glossary.en: sun zhi you sun - loss upon loss
glossary.note: To keep on reducing, getting rid of all contrivance.

glossary.en: wu shi - freedom from meddling
glossary.note: Not stirring up trouble and not disturbing the people.

glossary.en: wuwei er wu bu wei - non-action and nothing left undone
glossary.note: See chapter 37.

ch49.summary: The sage has no fixed heart of his own and takes the people's heart as his heart. He is good to the good and also to the not good, and trusts the trustworthy and also the untrustworthy, so that hearts in the world return to simplicity.
ch49.translation:
The sage has no fixed heart; he takes the hearts of the people as his heart.
To the good I am good, and to the not good I am also good: virtue is goodness. To the trustworthy I am trusting, and to the untrustworthy I am also trusting: virtue is trust.
The sage in the world draws himself in; for the world he makes his heart blend into one. The people all fix their ears and eyes on him, and the sage treats them all as children.

glossary.en: wu chang xin - no fixed heart
glossary.note: No fixed opinions; he changes with the people's wishes.

glossary.en: de shan, de xin - virtue is goodness, virtue is trust
glossary.note: Using virtue to transform people so that all become good and trusting. Some editions write a different character for 'de'.

glossary.en: xixi - drawn in
glossary.note: The look of someone restrained and gentle.

glossary.en: hun qi xin - blend the heart into one
glossary.note: To make the heart simple, without cleverness.

ch50.summary: People come out into life and go into death: three in ten are long-lived, three in ten are short-lived, and three in ten seek their own death. One who is good at caring for life does not enter the land of death.
ch50.translation:
Coming out into life, going into death. Three in ten are followers of life. Three in ten are followers of death. And among people who live, those whose movements take them to the land of death are also three in ten. Why? Because they feed on life too richly.
I have heard that one who is good at caring for his life does not meet rhinoceros or tiger when walking on land, and when he goes into an army he is not struck by weapons. The rhinoceros finds nowhere to thrust its horn, the tiger nowhere to set its claws, and the weapon nowhere to lodge its blade. Why? Because he has no place of death.

glossary.en: sheng zhi tu, si zhi tu - followers of life, followers of death
glossary.note: 'Tu' means kind or class. 'Shi you san' can be read as 'three in ten' or as 'thirteen'; another reading takes it as thirteen organs.

glossary.en: sheng sheng zhi hou - feeding on life too richly
glossary.note: Looking after oneself too lavishly in order to live.

glossary.en: she sheng - preserving life
glossary.note: Looking after life, keeping oneself in health.

glossary.en: si - rhinoceros
glossary.note: A fierce animal of the rhinoceros kind.

ch50.background: The phrase 'shi you san' has been explained in different ways. Wang Bi and others read it as three in ten; Han Feizi reads it as the four limbs and nine openings, thirteen in all. Both readings exist side by side.

ch51.summary: The Dao gives birth, virtue nourishes, things give form and circumstance completes. The ten thousand things honour the Dao and prize virtue not because they are ordered to, but naturally. The Dao gives life and nourishes without owning, and this is called mysterious virtue.
ch51.translation:
The Dao gives birth to them. Virtue nourishes them. Things give them form. Circumstances complete them. Therefore the ten thousand things all honour the Dao and prize virtue.
The honour of the Dao and the prize of virtue are not ordered by anyone, and are always natural. So the Dao gives birth to them and virtue nourishes them; it raises them and rears them, shapes them and ripens them, shelters them and covers them.
It gives life without owning, acts without relying, leads without ruling: this is called mysterious virtue.

glossary.en: de - virtue (de)
glossary.note: The Dao's concrete working and endowment in things; each thing receives its own de and so fulfils its nature.

glossary.en: shi - circumstances
glossary.note: Surroundings and conditions.

glossary.en: ting zhi du zhi - shape them, ripen them
glossary.note: 'Ting' is to give form and 'du' is to bring to ripeness: to settle and mature them.

glossary.en: xuande - mysterious virtue
glossary.note: See chapter 10.

ch52.summary: To know the Dao, the 'mother', is to be able to know the ten thousand things, her 'children'. Blocking the openings and shutting the doors, seeing the small and holding to softness, is the way of practising the constant.
ch52.translation:
The world had a beginning, which can be taken as the mother of the world. Having found the mother, one can know the children. Having known the children, one goes back to hold the mother, and to the end of life is free from danger.
Block the openings, shut the doors, and to the end of life there is no toil. Open the openings, add to your affairs, and to the end of life there is no rescue.
Seeing the small is called clarity. Holding to softness is called strength. Use its light and return to its clarity; do not leave disaster to your own person. This is called practising the constant.

glossary.en: mu, zi - mother, children
glossary.note: The mother is the Dao and the children are the ten thousand things.

glossary.en: sai qi dui, bi qi men - block the openings, shut the doors
glossary.note: 'Dui' is the mouth and by extension the openings of the senses; it means shutting the gates of craving.

glossary.en: jian xiao yue ming - seeing the small is called clarity
glossary.note: To see into things from their fine details is real understanding.

glossary.en: xi chang - practising the constant
glossary.note: To follow the unchanging law; 'xi' is the same as 'xi', to carry on.

ch53.summary: The great Way is level, yet people like side paths. Rulers live in splendour while the people go without; this is how robber chieftains behave, and it is not the Dao.
ch53.translation:
If I had even a little knowledge, I would walk the great Way, and fear only to stray off it. The great Way is very level, but people love the side paths.
The court is very clean, yet the fields are very overgrown and the granaries very empty. They wear embroidered clothes, carry sharp swords, are sated with food and drink, and have more goods than they need. This is called robber chieftains. It is not the Dao!

glossary.en: jieran - slightly
glossary.note: In a small way, a little.

glossary.en: shi - side road
glossary.note: Read as 'yi', a crooked or evil path; it means a slanting road.

glossary.en: jing - path
glossary.note: A small road, a short cut.

glossary.en: dao kua - robber chieftain
glossary.note: 'Kua' means leader. The Han Feizi has 'robber piper' instead.

ch54.summary: What is well planted is not uprooted and what is well held does not slip. Cultivated from the person to the family, village, state and world, virtue grows and spreads.
ch54.translation:
What is well planted is not uprooted. What is well held does not slip away. Sons and grandsons will offer sacrifice without end.
Cultivate it in yourself, and its virtue will be genuine. Cultivate it in the family, and its virtue will overflow. Cultivate it in the village, and its virtue will grow long. Cultivate it in the state, and its virtue will be abundant. Cultivate it in the world, and its virtue will be universal.
So judge a person by the person, a family by the family, a village by the village, a state by the state, the world by the world. How do I know that the world is so? By this.

glossary.en: shan jian, shan bao - well planted, well held
glossary.note: One who is good at establishing virtue and holding to the great Dao cannot be robbed of it.

glossary.en: xiu zhi yu shen - cultivate it in yourself
glossary.note: Self-cultivation is the root and extends to family, village, state and world. The order is close to that of the Great Learning (Daxue).

glossary.en: yi shen guan shen - judge a person by the person
glossary.note: To judge each level by looking at that level itself, and so understand all of them by analogy.

glossary.en: yu, chang, feng, pu - overflowing, long, abundant, universal
glossary.note: The way virtue widens step by step in the family, village, state and world.

ch55.summary: A person who holds virtue in full is like a newborn child: poisonous creatures and fierce beasts do not harm him, his bones are soft yet his grip is firm, and his vital essence is pure and harmonious. One who knows harmony and the constant is clear, but forcing life, or letting the mind drive the qi, only brings early decline.
ch55.translation:
One who holds virtue in fullness is like a newborn child. Wasps, scorpions, vipers and snakes do not sting him. Fierce beasts do not seize him. Birds of prey do not strike him.
His bones are weak and his sinews soft, yet his grip is firm. He does not yet know the union of male and female, yet his body stirs: this is the utmost of vital essence. He cries all day without growing hoarse: this is the utmost of harmony.
To know harmony is called the constant. To know the constant is called clarity. To add to life is called ominous. For the mind to drive the qi is called forcing.
When things are strong they grow old. This is called against the Dao, and what is against the Dao comes early to its end.

glossary.en: chizi - newborn child
glossary.note: A baby just born.

glossary.en: fengchai huishe - wasps, scorpions, vipers and snakes
glossary.note: Stinging insects and poisonous snakes.

glossary.en: sha - hoarse
glossary.note: A voice that has become rough.

glossary.en: yi sheng yue xiang - adding to life is ominous
glossary.note: To try to add to life by force is a bad omen. 'Xiang' here means a sign of evil or calamity.

ch56.summary: The wise do not talk much, and those who talk much are not necessarily wise. Putting away craving, blunting the sharp, untying tangles and joining the dust, one becomes mysteriously one with the Dao, and so is not swayed by closeness or distance, gain or harm, honour or disgrace.
ch56.translation:
One who knows does not speak; one who speaks does not know.
Block the openings, shut the doors, blunt the sharp, untie the tangles, soften the glare, join the dust: this is called mysterious sameness. So one cannot be made close and cannot be made distant. One cannot be benefited and cannot be harmed. One cannot be honoured and cannot be disgraced. Therefore he is honoured by the world.

glossary.en: zhi zhe bu yan - one who knows does not speak
glossary.note: True knowing does not lie in speech. It echoes 'a Dao that can be spoken is not the constant Dao' in chapter 1.

glossary.en: he guang tong chen - soften the glare, join the dust
glossary.note: To hide one's edge and blend in with the world. It became a well-known maxim for how to live.

glossary.en: xuantong - mysterious sameness
glossary.note: A mysterious unity with the Dao, without distinction.

glossary.en: jie qi fen - untie the tangles
glossary.note: The same as 'untie the tangles' in chapter 4; Wang Bi's text writes a different character.
