ch57.summary: Govern a state with correctness, use troops with surprise, and win the world by not meddling. The more laws there are, the more thieves there are; the sage does not act, and the people transform of themselves.
ch57.translation:
Govern a state with correctness. Use troops with surprise. Win the world by not meddling. How do I know it is so? By this:
The more taboos and prohibitions there are in the world, the poorer the people become. The more sharp weapons the people have, the darker the state grows. The more skills and cleverness people have, the more strange things appear. The more laws and decrees are displayed, the more robbers and thieves there are.
Therefore the sage says: I do not act, and the people transform of themselves. I love stillness, and the people become upright of themselves. I do not meddle, and the people become rich of themselves. I have no desire, and the people become simple of themselves.

glossary.en: yi zheng zhi guo, yi qi yong bing - govern with correctness, use troops with surprise
glossary.note: 'Zheng' is the upright way and 'qi' is surprise and trickery: in ruling use correctness, in war surprise may be used.

glossary.en: jihui - taboos and prohibitions
glossary.note: Bans and prohibitions.

glossary.en: liqi - sharp tools
glossary.note: Sharp weapons, or else the arts of scheming and technique.

glossary.en: jiqiao - skill and cleverness
glossary.note: Technique, cleverness.

ch58.summary: A mild government makes the people honest; a prying one makes them cunning. Disaster and good fortune lean on and hide in each other with no fixed standard, and the sage is upright without wounding.
ch58.translation:
When the government is dull and muddled, the people are honest and simple. When the government is sharp and prying, the people are cunning and lacking.
Disaster is what good fortune leans on; good fortune is what disaster hides in. Who knows where it ends? There is no fixed standard. The upright turns again into the strange, and the good turns again into the ominous. People's confusion has lasted a long time.
Therefore the sage is square but does not cut, has edges but does not pierce, is straight but does not run wild, is bright but does not dazzle.

glossary.en: menmen, chunchun - dull and muddled, honest and simple
glossary.note: 'Menmen' is a generous, plain way of governing, and 'chunchun' is the plainness of the people.

glossary.en: chacha, queque - sharp and prying, cunning and lacking
glossary.note: 'Chacha' is harsh and exacting scrutiny, and 'quequek' is slyness and deceit.

glossary.en: huo fu xiang yi - disaster and good fortune lean on each other
glossary.note: Laozi's dialectical thought, behind the story of the old man at the frontier who lost his horse, which gave rise to the saying.

glossary.en: fang er bu ge, lian er bu gui - square but not cutting, edged but not piercing
glossary.note: Upright without hurting others, with corners that do not prick.

ch59.summary: In governing people and serving Heaven, nothing is better than thrift (sparing one's spirit and strength). Thrift leads to early submission, to accumulated virtue and to overcoming all, which is the Way of deep roots, a firm stem, long life and lasting vision.
ch59.translation:
In governing people and serving Heaven, nothing is better than thrift. Only thrift can be called early submission. Early submission is called repeated accumulation of virtue. With repeated accumulation of virtue, nothing cannot be overcome. When nothing cannot be overcome, no one knows his limit. When no one knows his limit, he can hold a state. One who holds the mother of the state can last long.
This is called deep roots and a firm stem, the Way of long life and lasting vision.

glossary.en: se - thrift
glossary.note: Being sparing and economical, especially sparing of spirit and strength.

glossary.en: zao fu - early submission
glossary.note: Submitting early to the Dao.

glossary.en: zhong ji de - repeated accumulation of virtue
glossary.note: Storing up virtue and then storing up more.

glossary.en: changsheng jiushi - long life and lasting vision
glossary.note: To make life long. 'Jiushi' means to last for a long time.

ch60.summary: Govern a great state as you cook a small fish, without turning it over too often. When the world is governed by the Dao, spirits have no power, the sage does not harm people either, and virtue returns to the people.
ch60.translation: Govern a great state as you would cook a small fish. When the world is governed with the Dao, the ghosts have no power. It is not that the ghosts have no power, but their power does not harm people. It is not that their power does not harm people, but the sage does not harm people either. When neither harms the other, virtue returns to both.

glossary.en: peng xiaoxian - cook a small fish
glossary.note: Small fish must not be turned over too much when cooked: a picture of governing with non-action and not disturbing the people.

glossary.en: li - to oversee
glossary.note: To face, to govern.

glossary.en: qi gui bu shen - the ghosts have no power
glossary.note: The spirits show no efficacy, so there are no hauntings.

glossary.en: de jiao gui - virtue returns to both
glossary.note: Virtue comes together and returns to the people.

ch61.summary: A great state should be humble like the lower reaches of a river, and so win small states. A small state should also take the lower place before a great one; each gets what it wants, but the great one should especially keep below.
ch61.translation:
A great state is the lower reaches of a river, the meeting place of the world, the female of the world. The female always overcomes the male by stillness, and takes the lower place in stillness.
So if a great state places itself below a small state, it wins the small state. If a small state places itself below a great state, it wins the great state. So some place themselves below in order to win, and some win because they are below.
A great state wants no more than to unite and nurture people. A small state wants no more than to join and serve others. For both to get what they want, the great one should take the lower place.

glossary.en: xialiu - lower reaches
glossary.note: The lower part of a river, which lies low and gathers a hundred streams.

glossary.en: pin - the female
glossary.note: The female, a picture of soft stillness and the lower place.

glossary.en: xia - to be humble
glossary.note: To take a humble attitude and the lower place.

glossary.en: jianxu - to unite and nurture
glossary.note: To bring together and look after; another view reads it as gathering and raising.

ch62.summary: The Dao is the hidden depth of the ten thousand things; the good treasure it and the not-good take refuge in it. What can be offered to others is not treasure but 'to offer this Dao'.
ch62.translation:
The Dao is the hidden depth of the ten thousand things. It is the treasure of the good person and the refuge of the not-good.
Fine words can be traded. Honoured conduct can be added to others. Why should anyone be cast away because he is not good?
Therefore when an emperor is set up and the three ministers are appointed, though one offers a great jade disc ahead of a team of four horses, it is better to sit and offer this Dao.
Why did the ancients prize this Dao? Did they not say: seek and find it, and the guilty are forgiven? So it is honoured by the world.

glossary.en: ao - the hidden depth
glossary.note: The deep inner part, or a place of shelter, a place to hide.

glossary.en: meiyan keyi shi - fine words can be traded
glossary.note: Wang Bi reads it as 'fine words can be traded, honoured conduct can be added to others'. Others (Heshang Gong and so on) read it as 'fine words can buy honour, fine deeds can be added to others'. Either way it means that fine words and deeds win respect and put one above others.

glossary.en: gongbi, sima - jade disc, team of four horses
glossary.note: A 'gongbi' is a large jade disc that takes both hands to hold, and 'sima' is a carriage drawn by four horses: both are precious gifts.

glossary.en: zuo jin ci dao - sit and offer this Dao
glossary.note: To present this Dao while sitting; it means one gets it without effort.

ch63.summary: Handle things with non-action, plan the hard while it is easy and do the great while it is small. One who promises lightly keeps few promises; the sage treats things as hard, and so in the end has no difficulty.
ch63.translation:
Act without acting. Work without working. Taste the tasteless. Whether big or small, many or few, repay resentment with virtue.
Plan for the difficult while it is easy; do the great while it is small. The difficult things of the world must start from the easy; the great things of the world must start from the small. Therefore the sage never does anything great, and so he can accomplish the great.
One who lightly promises is sure to keep few promises; one who thinks everything easy is sure to meet many difficulties. Therefore the sage treats even easy things as difficult, and so in the end he has no difficulties.

glossary.en: wei wuwei, shi wushi, wei wuwei - act without acting, work without working, taste the tasteless
glossary.note: To deal with everything in the spirit of non-action, non-meddling and plainness.

glossary.en: bao yuan yi de - repay resentment with virtue
glossary.note: To answer hatred with kindness. In the Analects (Xianwen) Confucius took a different view: 'repay resentment with uprightness, and virtue with virtue'.

glossary.en: tu nan yu qi yi - plan for the difficult while it is easy
glossary.note: To begin while a difficulty can still be handled.

glossary.en: qing nuo bi gua xin - one who promises lightly keeps few promises
glossary.note: What is lightly agreed to often cannot be done.

ch64.summary: Deal with things before disorder arises: a journey of a thousand li begins beneath one's feet. Do not act on it, do not grasp it, be as careful at the end as at the beginning, and help the ten thousand things be natural.
ch64.translation:
What is at peace is easy to hold. What has not yet shown signs is easy to plan for. What is brittle is easy to break. What is tiny is easy to scatter. Act on it before it exists; put it in order before there is disorder.
A tree of arm's span grows from a tiny shoot. A tower of nine storeys rises from a heap of earth. A journey of a thousand li begins beneath one's feet.
Whoever acts ruins it; whoever grasps it loses it. So the sage does not act, and therefore does not ruin; he does not grasp, and therefore does not lose. In their undertakings, people often fail when they are nearly done. Be as careful at the end as at the beginning, and there will be no failed undertakings.
Therefore the sage desires not to desire, and does not prize goods that are hard to get; he learns not to learn, and goes back to what the many have passed by. He helps the ten thousand things to be natural, and does not dare to act.

glossary.en: haomo - tiny tip
glossary.note: A fine, small shoot.

glossary.en: leitu - heaped earth
glossary.note: Earth piled up basket by basket. The word is also written with a different character meaning a basket of earth.

glossary.en: qianli zhi xing, shi yu zu xia - a journey of a thousand li begins beneath one's feet
glossary.note: The source of this saying: great things start from small ones, and one should not fear the difficulty.

glossary.en: shen zhong ru shi - be as careful at the end as at the beginning
glossary.note: Be as careful at the end as one was at the start.

ch65.summary: Those of old who were good at the Dao did not make the people clever but kept them simple. To govern a state by cleverness is to rob the state; not to do so is a blessing for it.
ch65.translation:
Those of old who were good at practising the Dao did not use it to make the people clear-minded, but to make them simple. The people are hard to govern because they have too much cleverness. So to govern a state by cleverness is a robber of the state; not to govern a state by cleverness is a blessing for the state.
To know these two is also to know a pattern. Always to know the pattern is called mysterious virtue. Mysterious virtue is deep and far-reaching; it is the opposite of things, and only then does it reach complete accord.

glossary.en: yu zhi - to make them simple
glossary.note: This does not mean to fool them but to bring them back to simplicity and away from cunning tricks.

glossary.en: jishi - a pattern
glossary.note: A rule or model.

glossary.en: xuande - mysterious virtue
glossary.note: See chapters 10 and 51.

glossary.en: da shun - complete accord
glossary.note: The greatest harmony, that is, going along with nature.

ch66.summary: Rivers and seas are kings of the hundred valleys because they are good at staying below. A sage who wants to be above the people must speak humbly to them, and one who wants to lead must put himself behind; because he does not contend, no one can contend with him.
ch66.translation:
The reason rivers and seas can be kings of the hundred valleys is that they are good at being below, and so they can be kings of the hundred valleys.
Therefore, wishing to be above the people, one must speak humbly to them. Wishing to be ahead of the people, one must put oneself behind them. So the sage stands above and the people do not feel him a burden; he stands in front and the people are not harmed. Therefore the whole world is glad to push him forward and does not tire of him. Because he does not contend, no one in the world can contend with him.

glossary.en: bai gu wang - king of the hundred valleys
glossary.note: The king to whom all the streams of the valleys flow: the rivers and the sea.

glossary.en: shan xia - good at being below
glossary.note: Skilled at taking the lower place.

glossary.en: yi yan xia zhi, yi shen hou zhi - speak humbly, put oneself behind
glossary.note: Humble in words and in the rear in action.

glossary.en: le tui bu yan - glad to push forward and never tired
glossary.note: The people are glad to raise him up and do not weary of it.

ch67.summary: Laozi says he has three treasures: compassion, frugality, and not daring to be first in the world. Through compassion there is courage, through frugality there is breadth, through staying behind one becomes chief; compassion wins in attack and holds firm in defence.
ch67.translation:
Everyone in the world says my Dao is great, yet it seems like nothing. It is just because it is great that it seems like nothing. If it were like something, it would long ago have become small!
I have three treasures, which I hold and keep. The first is compassion. The second is frugality. The third is not daring to be first in the world. Being compassionate, one can be brave. Being frugal, one can be broad. Not daring to be first in the world, one can become chief of vessels.
Now people give up compassion and seek courage, give up frugality and seek breadth, give up staying behind and seek to be first: this is death! Compassion wins in attack and holds firm in defence. When Heaven is about to save someone, it guards him with compassion.

glossary.en: bu xiao - like nothing
glossary.note: Not resembling anything: the Dao is too great to be compared with any particular thing.

glossary.en: sanbao - three treasures
glossary.note: Compassion, frugality and not daring to be first in the world: Laozi's three principles for living.

glossary.en: cheng qi zhang - chief of vessels
glossary.note: To become the head of all things or of all officials. 'Qi' means things and 'zhang' means chief.

glossary.en: ci gu neng yong - through compassion, courage
glossary.note: Courage that grows from real love lasts longer than courage that shows off strength.

ch68.summary: A good commander does not parade his force, a good fighter is not quick to anger, a good winner does not meet the enemy head on, and a good user of men is humble. This is called the virtue of not contending.
ch68.translation:
One who is good at being an officer is not warlike. One who is good at fighting is not angry. One who is good at conquering enemies does not engage them. One who is good at using people puts himself below them.
This is called the virtue of not contending. This is called using the strength of others. This is called matching Heaven, the ancient ultimate.

glossary.en: shi - officer
glossary.note: A warrior or commander.

glossary.en: bu yu - not engaging
glossary.note: Not meeting head on and not contending.

glossary.en: wei zhi xia - putting oneself below
glossary.note: To be humble before others.

glossary.en: pei tian - matching Heaven
glossary.note: To be in accord with the Way of Heaven.

ch69.summary: Those who use troops hold to defence and do not look down on the enemy; underestimating the enemy is the worst disaster. When two armies are equal in strength, the side that feels compassion wins.
ch69.translation:
There is a saying among those who use troops: "I dare not play host but play guest; I dare not advance an inch but retreat a foot." This is called marching without lines, rolling up sleeves without arms, seizing without an enemy, holding without weapons.
No calamity is greater than underestimating the enemy; underestimating the enemy nearly loses my treasures. Therefore when armies meet in equal strength, the one that grieves wins.

glossary.en: wei zhu, wei ke - to be host, to be guest
glossary.note: The host is the one who attacks on his own initiative, and the guest is the one who responds when attacked.

glossary.en: xing wu xing, rang wu bi - march without lines, roll up sleeves without arms
glossary.note: 'Xing' is a line or formation and 'rang' is to roll up one's sleeves: both mean not showing one's edge.

glossary.en: qing di ji sang wu bao - underestimating the enemy nearly loses my treasures
glossary.note: To look down on the enemy would almost cost me my three treasures (compassion, frugality, not daring to be first).

glossary.en: kang bing xiang jia, ai zhe sheng - armies meet, the grieving win
glossary.note: When strength is equal, the side with compassion wins.

ch70.summary: Laozi's words are easy to understand and practise, yet no one in the world can understand or practise them. Since few know him, he is the more precious; the sage wears coarse cloth and carries jade within.
ch70.translation:
My words are very easy to understand and very easy to practise. Yet no one in the world can understand them, and no one can practise them.
Words have an ancestor, and affairs have a lord. It is just because people do not know this that they do not know me. Those who know me are few, and those who take me as a model are precious. Therefore the sage wears coarse cloth and carries jade within his bosom.

glossary.en: yan you zong, shi you jun - words have an ancestor, affairs have a lord
glossary.note: Speech has its guiding purpose and affairs have their master, meaning the Dao.

glossary.en: ze wo zhe gui - those who take me as model are precious
glossary.note: Those who can follow my example are rare and precious. 'Ze' here means to take as a model.

glossary.en: bei he huai yu - wear coarse cloth and carry jade
glossary.note: Dressed in rough clothes with jade held close to the heart: plain outside and gifted within.

glossary.en: fu wei wu zhi - only because they do not know
glossary.note: It means that people do not truly understand.

ch71.summary: To know that one does not know is best. Only by treating faults as faults does one avoid faults.
ch71.translation:
To know that one does not know is best. Not to know, and to think that one knows, is a sickness.
Only one who is sick of the sickness is not sick. The sage is not sick: because he is sick of the sickness, he is not sick.

glossary.en: zhi bu zhi shang - to know that one does not know is best
glossary.note: To know the limit of one's knowledge is best. It echoes the Analects: 'to know what you know and know what you do not know, that is knowledge'.

glossary.en: bing - sickness, fault
glossary.note: A fault, a defect.

glossary.en: fu wei bing bing - only by taking the sickness as sickness
glossary.note: Precisely because one treats the fault as a fault.

glossary.en: bu zhi zhi, bing - not knowing and thinking one knows is a sickness
glossary.note: Not knowing but believing that one knows is the real fault.

ch72.summary: If rulers do not make the people feel awe, a great disaster will come. Do not press upon where people live or weigh down how they make a living; the sage knows himself but does not show himself, and loves himself but does not exalt himself.
ch72.translation:
When the people do not fear authority, then a great terror comes. Do not narrow the places where they live. Do not oppress how they make their living. Only if you do not oppress them will they not tire of you.
Therefore the sage knows himself but does not show himself; he loves himself but does not exalt himself. So he leaves that and takes this.

glossary.en: min bu wei wei - the people do not fear authority
glossary.note: When the people are no longer afraid of the ruler's power, they may rise in revolt.

glossary.en: xia - to press in
glossary.note: Written for the word meaning narrow; it means to squeeze.

glossary.en: yan - to oppress, to tire of
glossary.note: The first 'yan' is to weigh down on, and the second is to be tired of.

glossary.en: zizhi bu zixian - knows himself but does not show himself
glossary.note: Knowing oneself and not putting oneself on show.

ch73.summary: One who is brave in daring is killed; one who is brave in not daring lives. The Way of Heaven wins without contending, answers without speaking, and its net is wide yet lets nothing through.
ch73.translation:
One who is brave in daring is killed. One who is brave in not daring lives. Of these two, one brings benefit and one brings harm. Who knows why Heaven dislikes what it dislikes? Therefore even the sage finds it hard.
The Way of Heaven does not contend and yet wins well; does not speak and yet answers well; is not summoned and yet comes of itself; is relaxed and yet plans well.
The net of Heaven is vast; its mesh is wide, yet nothing slips through.

glossary.en: yong yu gan, yong yu bu gan - brave in daring, brave in not daring
glossary.note: The first is rash boldness and the second is humble restraint.

glossary.en: chanran - relaxed
glossary.note: Easy and unhurried.

glossary.en: tianwang huihui, shu er bu shi - the net of Heaven is vast, wide yet nothing slips through
glossary.note: The source of this saying. The Way of Heaven is vast, and though it seems loose it lets no evil deed escape.

glossary.en: you nan zhi - even the sage finds it hard
glossary.note: Even the sage finds it hard to judge.

ch74.summary: If the people do not fear death, threatening them with death is useless. Killing belongs to the Way of Heaven; to kill on its behalf is like cutting wood for the master carpenter, and few do not hurt their own hands.
ch74.translation:
If the people do not fear death, why frighten them with death? Suppose the people always feared death, and I could seize and kill those who do strange things - who would dare?
There is always one who has charge of killing. To kill in the place of the one who has charge of killing is called cutting wood in place of the master carpenter. Of those who cut in place of the master carpenter, few do not hurt their own hands.

glossary.en: min bu wei si - the people do not fear death
glossary.note: Under harsh rule life is no better than death, and so the people stop fearing it.

glossary.en: si sha zhe - the one who has charge of killing
glossary.note: The one in charge of killing: the Way of Heaven or the law of nature.

glossary.en: da jiang zhuo - the master carpenter cutting
glossary.note: A skilled carpenter cutting and trimming wood.

glossary.en: naihe yi si ju zhi - why frighten them with death
glossary.note: It is close in meaning to 'harsh government is fiercer than a tiger' in the Book of Rites.

ch75.summary: The people go hungry because their rulers tax too much, are hard to govern because their rulers meddle, and take death lightly because their rulers live too richly. Those who do not live for the sake of living are wiser than those who prize life.
ch75.translation:
The people are hungry because those above eat up so much in taxes; that is why they are hungry. The people are hard to govern because those above meddle; that is why they are hard to govern. The people take death lightly because those above seek life too richly; that is why they take death lightly.
Only those who do not act for the sake of life are wiser than those who prize life.

glossary.en: shi shui - eating taxes
glossary.note: To consume what is taken in taxes; to levy taxes.

glossary.en: youwei - meddling
glossary.note: Meaning that the ruler acts rashly and does too much.

glossary.en: qiu sheng zhi hou - seeking life too richly
glossary.note: Indulging oneself too lavishly.

glossary.en: gui sheng - prizing life
glossary.note: Valuing the pleasures of life too much.

ch76.summary: A living person is soft and a dead one is stiff, and it is the same with grass and trees. So the hard and strong belong with death, the soft and weak with life, and the strong and big stay below.
ch76.translation:
A person is born soft and weak, and at death is hard and stiff. The ten thousand things, the grass and trees, are born soft and tender, and at death are dry and brittle.
So the hard and stiff are the companions of death, and the soft and weak are the companions of life. Therefore an army that is strong does not win; a tree that is strong is cut down. The strong and big stay below; the soft and weak stay above.

glossary.en: rouruo, jianqiang - soft and weak, hard and strong
glossary.note: Laozi's central contrast: softness stands for life and vitality, hardness for rigidity and death.

glossary.en: si zhi tu, sheng zhi tu - companions of death, companions of life
glossary.note: 'Tu' means kind or class.

glossary.en: bing qiang ze bu sheng - a strong army does not win
glossary.note: A strong army tends to underestimate the enemy and lose. One reading changes 'win' to 'be destroyed'.

glossary.en: mu qiang ze bing - a strong tree is cut down
glossary.note: A sturdy tree is felled. Some texts read 'bing' differently, as 'together' or 'broken'.

ch77.summary: The Way of Heaven takes from what has too much and gives to what lacks, like drawing a bow; the way of people is the opposite. Only one who has the Dao can offer his surplus to the world, and the sage acts without relying on it and completes without dwelling in it.
ch77.translation:
The Way of Heaven is like drawing a bow, is it not? What is high is pressed down; what is low is lifted up. What has too much is reduced; what is lacking is made up. The Way of Heaven takes from what has excess and makes up what is lacking.
The way of people is not so. It takes from what is lacking to serve what has excess. Who can use his excess to serve the world? Only one who has the Dao.
Therefore the sage acts without relying on it, completes the work without dwelling in it, and does not wish to show his worth.

glossary.en: zhang gong - drawing a bow
glossary.note: When a bow is drawn, the high end is pressed down and the low end raised: a picture of balancing and adjusting.

glossary.en: sun youyu er bu bu zu - take from excess and make up what is lacking
glossary.note: The principle of balance in the Way of Heaven.

glossary.en: feng - to offer
glossary.note: To present, to give for others' use.

glossary.en: bu yu xian xian - not wishing to show worth
glossary.note: Not wanting to show off one's own ability.

ch78.summary: Nothing in the world is softer than water, yet nothing beats it at wearing down the hard and strong. Everyone knows that the soft overcomes the hard, but no one practises it; one who takes on the shame of the state becomes king of the world. 'Straight words seem to be their opposite.'
ch78.translation:
Nothing in the world is softer or weaker than water, yet in attacking the hard and strong nothing can surpass it, since nothing can take its place.
That the weak overcomes the strong and the soft overcomes the hard, everyone in the world knows, yet no one can practise it.
Therefore the sage says: "One who takes upon himself the filth of the state is called lord of the altars of the land and grain. One who takes upon himself the misfortunes of the state is king of the world." Straight words seem to be their opposite.

glossary.en: shui - water
glossary.note: For Laozi water is the symbol of what is soft and weak and yet overcomes the hard and strong. See chapter 8.

glossary.en: shou guo zhi gou - to take upon oneself the filth of the state
glossary.note: To bear the shame and the dirt of the country.

glossary.en: sheji zhu - lord of the altars of the land and grain
glossary.note: Master of the state. 'Sheji' is the god of the soil and the god of grain, and stands for the state.

glossary.en: zheng yan ruo fan - straight words seem opposite
glossary.note: True words seem to go against common sense.

ch79.summary: Even when a great grievance is settled, some resentment remains, so the sage keeps the debtor's tally and does not press for payment. Those with virtue keep the tally, those without collect; the Way of Heaven has no favourites and always helps the good.
ch79.translation:
When a great grievance is reconciled, some grievance is sure to remain. How can this be counted as good?
Therefore the sage holds the left half of the tally and does not press people for payment. One with virtue takes charge of the tally; one without virtue takes charge of collecting.
The Way of Heaven has no favourites; it is always with the good person.

glossary.en: zuo qi - the left half of the tally
glossary.note: In ancient times a contract tally was split into a left and a right half, and the creditor held the left half to claim a debt.

glossary.en: si qi, si che - in charge of the tally, in charge of collecting
glossary.note: One keeps the contract without pressing for the debt; the other collects taxes ('che' was the tax system of the Zhou).

glossary.en: tian dao wu qin - the Way of Heaven has no favourites
glossary.note: The Way of Heaven has no partiality and no closer or more distant relatives.

glossary.en: yu shan ren - with the good person
glossary.note: Helping the good.

ch80.summary: It draws the ideal of a small state with few people: simple and content, not valuing clever tools, and not moving about; though the neighbouring state is in sight, they grow old and die without visiting each other.
ch80.translation:
A small state with few people. Let there be tools worth ten or a hundred men and yet not use them. Let the people take death seriously and not move far away. Though there are boats and carriages, there is no occasion to ride them; though there are armour and weapons, there is no occasion to display them.
Let the people go back to knotted cords and use them. Let them find their food sweet, their clothes beautiful, their homes peaceful, their customs happy.
Neighbouring states may look across to each other, and the sounds of cocks and dogs may be heard from one to the other, yet the people grow old and die without going back and forth.

glossary.en: shi bai zhi qi - tools worth ten or a hundred men
glossary.note: Implements with ten or a hundred times a person's ability; another reading takes them to be weapons.

glossary.en: jie sheng - knotted cords
glossary.note: In remote antiquity people kept records by tying knots in cords, a sign of a simple life.

glossary.en: zhong si - to take death seriously
glossary.note: To value death, which is to cherish life.

glossary.en: lao si bu xiang wanglai - grow old and die without going back and forth
glossary.note: This is not isolation. Each lives content in its own place and no quarrels arise.

ch80.background: This chapter is seen as Laozi's political ideal, and also as a criticism of the disorder of the Warring States. Later, Tao Yuanming's 'Peach Blossom Spring' echoes it at a distance.

ch81.summary: The conclusion of the whole book: true words are not beautiful, the good do not argue, one with the Dao does not store things up and has more the more he does for others. The Way of Heaven benefits and does not harm; the Way of the sage acts and does not contend.
ch81.translation:
True words are not beautiful; beautiful words are not true. The good do not argue; those who argue are not good. Those who know are not learned; the learned do not know.
The sage does not store things up. The more he does for others, the more he has; the more he gives to others, the more he has.
The Way of Heaven benefits and does not harm. The Way of the sage acts and does not contend.

glossary.en: xin yan bu mei - true words are not beautiful
glossary.note: Words that are real and trustworthy are not always fine-sounding.

glossary.en: bian - to argue
glossary.note: To dispute, to argue cleverly.

glossary.en: bu ji - not storing up
glossary.note: Not piling up goods, not possessing.

glossary.en: li er bu hai, wei er bu zheng - benefits and does not harm, acts and does not contend
glossary.note: The book ends with the Way of Heaven and the Way of the sage.

ch81.background: This is the last chapter in Wang Bi's edition, and serves as a summing up of the whole book.
